```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
using CSV, DataFrames, Statistics, StatsBase, Dates, Printf, TOML, Markdown
using CairoMakie
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png", px_per_unit = 2)
set_theme!(
    theme_minimal();
    fontsize = 13,
    Axis = (xgridcolor = (:black, 0.08), ygridcolor = (:black, 0.08)),
    Legend = (framevisible = false,),
)

const RUN = get(ENV, "AEM_BENCHMARK_RUN", joinpath(homedir(), "aem_validation", "ldc-2025"))
const AN = joinpath(RUN, "analysis")
const REGIONS = ["NSW1", "QLD1", "SA1", "TAS1", "VIC1"]
const REGION_COLOR = Dict(zip(REGIONS, Makie.wong_colors()[1:5]))
const NEMPY = (mean = 0.13818, median = 0.0, p5 = -0.13336, p95 = 0.01353)

const TIMECOLS = ["SETTLEMENTDATE", "interval", "DateTime"]
function rd(name; dir = AN)
    df = CSV.read(joinpath(dir, name), DataFrame; stringtype = String, types = Dict(c => String for c in TIMECOLS), validate = false)
    for c in TIMECOLS
        c in names(df) && (df[!, c] = DateTime.(df[!, c], dateformat"yyyy-mm-ddTHH:MM:SS"))
    end
    return df
end
prices = rd("price_errors.csv")
rt = rd("interval_runtimes.csv")
disp = rd("dispatch_errors.csv")
fcas = rd("fcas_errors.csv")
ic = rd("interconnector_errors.csv")
viol = rd("constraint_violations.csv")
ldc = rd("load_duration_curve.csv"; dir = RUN)
manifest = TOML.parsefile(joinpath(AN, "manifest.toml"))
# Runner-overhead measurement: the same sampled intervals on disk-backed and in-memory time series.
const AB = get(ENV, "AEM_RUNTIME_AB_RUN", joinpath(homedir(), "aem_validation", "runtime-ab"))

# Markdown pipe table of a DataFrame: no type row, no row numbers, 4 significant digits.
function mdtable(df::AbstractDataFrame)
    cell(x) = ismissing(x) ? "–" : x isa AbstractFloat ? (isnan(x) ? "" : (x == round(x) && abs(x) < 1.0e6 ? string(Int(x)) : @sprintf("%.4g", x))) :
        x isa DateTime ? replace(string(x), "T" => " ") : string(x)
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ", join(replace.(names(df), "_" => " "), " | "), " |")
    println(io, "|", join(fill(" --- |", ncol(df))))
    for r in eachrow(df)
        println(io, "| ", join((cell(r[c]) for c in names(df)), " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

# Number formatting for inline text.
f1(x) = @sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2(x) = @sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3(x) = @sprintf("%.3f", x)
f4(x) = @sprintf("%.4f", x)
pct(x; d = 1) = @sprintf("%.*f%%", d, 100x)
fint(x) = replace(string(round(Int, x)), r"(?<=\d)(?=(\d{3})+$)" => ",")
q(v, p) = quantile(collect(skipmissing(v)), p)
isfin(x) = !ismissing(x) && isfinite(x)

e = filter(isfinite, prices.error_rop)
ae = abs.(e)
EXACT = 1.0e-3
const PHASE_COLS = ["system_build_s", "simulation_build_s", "execute_s", "compare_s"]
STALL_S = 300.0
n_stall = count(>(STALL_S), rt.total_s)
stall_by_phase = [count(>(STALL_S), rt[!, c]) for c in PHASE_COLS]
med_total = median(rt.total_s)
n_prices, n_int = length(e), length(unique(prices.SETTLEMENTDATE))
exact_share = mean(ae .< EXACT)
nlarge = count(>(1.0), ae)
nint_large = length(unique(prices.SETTLEMENTDATE[abs.(prices.error_rop) .> 1.0]))
nint_diff = length(unique(prices.SETTLEMENTDATE[abs.(prices.error_rop) .> EXACT]))

# Dual-range probe (scripts/dual_range_probe.jl): the optimal-price range of each differing price.
const H_MW = ["0.0001", "0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1.0", "10.0"]
const DR_ORDER = ["degenerate (0.0001 MW)", "within 0.001 MW", "within 0.01 MW", "within 0.1 MW", "within 1 MW", "within 10 MW", "beyond 10 MW"]
# Smallest move at which the price is an optimal price of the model within that many MW of the operating point.
function dual_distance(r, col = :published)
    r.n_rows <= 0 && return "failed"
    p = r[col]
    for (h, label) in zip(H_MW, DR_ORDER)
        (r[Symbol("p_down_", h)] - EXACT <= p <= r[Symbol("p_up_", h)] + EXACT) && return label
    end
    return DR_ORDER[end]
end
# Re-runs of the probe append rows: keep a successful row per target, else the last row written.
dr_all = rd("dual_ranges.csv")
dr_all = unique(vcat(dr_all[dr_all.n_rows .<= 0, :], dr_all[dr_all.n_rows .> 0, :]), [:interval, :market, :region]; keep = :last)
dr_all.distance = [dual_distance(r) for r in eachrow(dr_all)]
failed = (dr_all.distance .== "failed") .| (dr_all.n_rows .<= 0)
bad_fixed = isequal.(dr_all.fixed_lp_matches, false)
n_failed = count(failed)
n_fixed_bad = count(bad_fixed .& (.!failed))
dr = dr_all[.!(failed .| bad_fixed), :]
dr.abs_error = abs.(dr.solved_benchmark .- dr.published)
dr.kind = ifelse.(dr.market .== "ENERGY", "energy", "FCAS")
n_probe = nrow(dr)
n_probe_int = length(unique(dr.interval))
n_degen = count(d -> d == DR_ORDER[1], dr.distance)
n_small = count(d -> d in DR_ORDER[2:3], dr.distance)
n_far = n_probe - n_degen - n_small
n_beyond10 = count(d -> d == DR_ORDER[7], dr.distance)
iv_worst = combine(groupby(dr, :interval), :distance => (v -> DR_ORDER[maximum(indexin(v, DR_ORDER))]) => :worst)
n_iv_degen = count(==(DR_ORDER[1]), iv_worst.worst)
bench_in_range = count(r -> dual_distance(r, :solved_benchmark) == DR_ORDER[1], eachrow(dr))
bench_out = filter(r -> dual_distance(r, :solved_benchmark) != DR_ORDER[1], dr)
bench_out_ints = join(Dates.format.(unique(bench_out.interval), dateformat"yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM"), ", ")
moved = filter(r -> abs(r.solved_rerun - r.solved_benchmark) >= EXACT, dr)
moved_to_pub = count(r -> abs(r.solved_rerun - r.published) < EXACT, eachrow(moved))
tasreg = filter(r -> r.region == "TAS1" && r.market in ("RAISEREG", "LOWERREG") && abs(r.abs_error - 1) < 0.02, dr)
n_tasreg_degen = count(d -> d == DR_ORDER[1], tasreg.distance)
lswap = filter(r -> r.market in ("LOWER6SEC", "LOWER60SEC"), dr)
n_lswap_degen = count(d -> d == DR_ORDER[1], lswap.distance)
lpairs = combine(groupby(lswap, [:interval, :region]), nrow => :n, [:solved_benchmark, :published] => ((s, p) -> sum(s .- p)) => :net_error)
n_lpairs = count(==(2), lpairs.n)
n_lpairs_opp = count(r -> r.n == 2 && abs(r.net_error) < EXACT, eachrow(lpairs))
mainland_raise = filter(r -> r.market in ("RAISE6SEC", "RAISE60SEC", "RAISE5MIN", "RAISE1SEC") && r.region != "TAS1", dr)
rest = filter(r -> r.distance != DR_ORDER[1], dr)
n_rest = nrow(rest)
n_rest_cont = count(r -> r.kind == "FCAS" && r.region != "TAS1" && occursin(r"SEC|MIN", r.market), eachrow(rest))
flat10 = count(r -> abs(r[Symbol("p_up_10.0")] - r[Symbol("p_down_10.0")]) < EXACT, eachrow(rest))
ergy_rest = filter(r -> r.kind == "energy", rest)
n_ergy_rest = nrow(ergy_rest)
n_ergy_10 = count(d -> d in DR_ORDER[5:6], ergy_rest.distance)
showcase = only(eachrow(filter(r -> r.region == "TAS1" && r.market == "ENERGY" && r.interval == DateTime("2025-07-07T12:15:00"), dr_all)))
sc_lo = showcase[Symbol("p_down_0.0001")]
sc_hi = showcase[Symbol("p_up_0.0001")]
sc_in = sc_lo - EXACT <= showcase.published <= sc_hi + EXACT
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

We benchmark the NEMDE replica in `AustralianElectricityMarketsSimulations` (a PowerSimulations.jl dispatch problem built from AEMO MMSDM data) against the dispatch outcomes AEMO published, following the interval-by-interval protocol of nempy [@gorman2022nempy]. Rather than a uniform random sample of intervals, we draw `{julia} fint(nrow(rt))` intervals of calendar year 2025, one at random from each of 1000 equal-count strata of the system-demand load duration curve, so that the sample represents the whole demand range, including the scarcity tail. Each interval is solved independently from AEMO's observed state, with NEMDE's two-run fast-start procedure where the interval contains a fast-start unit. Against the published regional reference price (ROP), `{julia} pct(exact_share)` of the `{julia} fint(n_prices)` regional prices agree to within 0.001 \$/MWh, the median error is exactly zero, and the mean signed error is `{julia} f3(mean(e))` \$/MWh (nempy: `{julia} NEMPY.mean`, on a different sample). Only `{julia} nint_large` of the `{julia} fint(n_int)` intervals have any price error above 1 \$/MWh. We trace the residual differences to three families: ties in the offer stack, genuine differences in the primal dispatch in a small set of intervals, and gaps in the source data. A direct test of whether each published price is an optimal price of our model finds that `{julia} pct(n_degen / n_probe; d = 0)` of the `{julia} fint(n_probe)` differing prices are optimal prices of the model within 0.0001 MW of its operating point, including `{julia} n_tasreg_degen` of the `{julia} nrow(tasreg)` Tasmanian regulation ties. For those prices the difference is not evidence of model error. The other `{julia} fint(n_rest)` prices are not, and `{julia} n_rest_cont` of them are mainland contingency FCAS prices. A full interval takes `{julia} f1(mean(rt.total_s))` s on average (median `{julia} f1(med_total)` s) with six solver processes sharing one machine; `{julia} pct(1 - mean(rt.execute_s) / mean(rt.total_s), d = 0)` of that is system and model construction rather than the solve, and `{julia} n_stall` intervals stall for more than five minutes (up to 35) in a single phase, which inflates the mean. We close by placing the work in the design of PowerSimulations.jl.

# Introduction

AEMO dispatches the National Electricity Market (NEM) every five minutes with NEMDE, a mixed-integer linear program over regional energy balance, interconnector flows and losses, frequency control ancillary services (FCAS) co-optimisation and thousands of network constraint equations. The inputs (offers, limits, constraint definitions) and the outcomes (dispatch targets, regional prices, constraint marginal values) are published in the MMSDM archive on NEMWEB [@aemo_mmsdm]. This transparency allows an open model to be validated against the real market, as nempy did for a Python implementation [@gorman2022nempy].

This report documents the same exercise for `AustralianElectricityMarkets.jl`, a Julia workspace that turns MMSDM data into PowerSystems.jl `System`s and solves NEM dispatch replicas of them with PowerSimulations.jl (PSI). We ask three questions.

1. **Accuracy.** How closely does the replica reproduce published prices, unit dispatch, FCAS prices and interconnector flows over a year of conditions?
2. **Cost.** How long does it take, and where does the time go?
3. **Residuals.** Where the replica differs from NEMDE, why?

A final section relates the benchmark to the architecture of PowerSimulations.jl.

# Method

## Data and model

All inputs come from the local MMSDM cache (Hive-partitioned parquet read through DuckDB), populated for 2025 by the data package. For each interval the system builder `nem_system(db, NEMDEConfiguration(); date_range)` writes every NEMDE input once: offers and bands, unit availability and ramp limits, observed telemetry, FCAS trapezia, regional demand, interconnector and loss models, generic constraints and their right-hand sides, and the constraint violation penalty factors. The simulation package never writes to the system; it reads these inputs, builds the dispatch decision model with `template_nemde`, and solves it. When the system contains a unit whose offer carries a fast-start inflexibility profile, the interval is solved as NEMDE does, in two runs: a commitment run and a dispatch run that holds fast-start units to their profile. Prices are the duals of the energy balance and FCAS rows of the final linear program with the integer decisions fixed, as in NEMDE and nempy.

The solver is HiGHS [@huangfu2018highs] with one thread, a relative MIP gap of $10^{-9}$ and an absolute gap of $10^{-10}$, driven through JuMP [@dunning2017jump] and PSI from Julia [@bezanson2017julia].

## Sampling on the load duration curve

nempy draws 1000 intervals uniformly at random from the five-minute grid of 2024 H2. A uniform draw rarely visits the few hundred highest-demand intervals, and these are precisely where binding constraints, scarcity and price spikes concentrate. We therefore rank all `{julia} fint(nrow(ldc))` complete intervals of 2025 (01 January 04:05 to 31 December 23:55) by total system demand, the sum over the five regions of the dispatched `TOTALDEMAND` in the non-intervention run, cut the ranking into 1000 equal-count strata, and draw one interval uniformly from each stratum with a fixed seed. Every demand decile is therefore represented by exactly 100 intervals.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ldc
#| fig-cap: "Load duration curve of 2025 total system demand (100 000+ five-minute intervals) with the 1000 sampled intervals, one per equal-count stratum. The sample follows the curve by construction, including its steep upper tail."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
let
    fig = Figure(size = (900, 420))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Rank (1 = highest demand)", ylabel = "System demand (MW)")
    step = 25
    lines!(ax, ldc.ldc_rank[1:step:end], ldc.system_demand_mw[1:step:end]; color = :gray40, linewidth = 2, label = "All 2025 intervals")
    smp = rd("ldc_sample.csv")
    scatter!(ax, smp.ldc_rank, smp.system_demand_mw; color = (:crimson, 0.55), markersize = 5, label = "Sampled (n = $(nrow(smp)))")
    axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
    fig
end
```

Eleven of the first draw (1.1%) fell on 2025-09-30 and 2025-10-01, where AEMO's September `DISPATCHLOAD` and `DISPATCH_MNSPBIDTRK` archive ends at 2025-09-30 04:00 (see @sec-data). They were replaced by new draws from the same strata on other trading days, so the final sample still has exactly one interval per stratum.

## Execution

The 1000 intervals were grouped by trading day into six shards and solved by six concurrent worker processes on one Apple M5 machine (10 cores, 32 GB). Each shard is a separate batch-runner process that started a fresh Julia worker process for each trading day and held the time series on disk, the runner's defaults at the time (@sec-overheads). For each interval the worker builds a system, builds the PSI decision models, solves, extracts results and compares them to the published tables, then discards the simulation folder. Intervals are independent: none starts from another's solution, only from AEMO's observed initial state. This is the same independent-solve protocol as the nempy benchmark. The run took about 8.5 hours of wall time.

## Comparison metrics

All comparisons are signed, solved minus published. Energy prices are compared with the regional reference price before post-dispatch adjustment (`ROP`), as nempy does. We also compare FCAS prices by service and region, dispatch targets (`TOTALCLEARED`) by unit, and interconnector flow and losses. Error summaries use the mean, median, 5th and 95th percentiles (the statistics nempy reports), plus mean absolute error and the share of values that agree to within 0.001 (prices, in \$/MWh) or 0.01 (flows, MW).

# Results: agreement with NEMDE

## Energy prices

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-nempy
#| tbl-cap: "Signed ROP error (solved minus published, \\$/MWh). nempy's figures are from its published 1000-interval benchmark of 2024 H2 and a uniform sample, so the comparison is indicative, not like-for-like."
let
    stats(v) = (n = length(v), mean = mean(v), median = median(v), p5 = q(v, 0.05), p95 = q(v, 0.95), mae = mean(abs, v), max_abs = maximum(abs, v))
    rows = DataFrame(
        source = ["nempy (2024 H2, uniform)", "AEMSim (2025, LDC-stratified)"],
        n = [missing, length(e)],
        mean = [NEMPY.mean, mean(e)], median = [NEMPY.median, median(e)],
        p5 = [NEMPY.p5, q(e, 0.05)], p95 = [NEMPY.p95, q(e, 0.95)],
        mae = [missing, mean(ae)], max_abs = [missing, maximum(ae)],
    )
    for r in REGIONS
        v = filter(isfinite, prices.error_rop[prices.REGIONID .== r])
        push!(rows, (; source = "AEMSim, $r", n = length(v), mean = mean(v), median = median(v), p5 = q(v, 0.05), p95 = q(v, 0.95), mae = mean(abs, v), max_abs = maximum(abs, v)))
    end
    mapcols!(c -> [ismissing(x) ? missing : (x isa AbstractFloat ? round(x; sigdigits = 4) : x) for x in c], rows)
    mdtable(rows)
end
```

`{julia} pct(exact_share)` of the `{julia} fint(n_prices)` regional prices are within 0.001 \$/MWh of the published ROP, and the 5th and 95th percentiles are essentially zero (@tbl-nempy). The mean error is positive (`{julia} f3(mean(e))` \$/MWh) and driven by a handful of intervals; the median is exactly 0. nempy reports a mean of `{julia} NEMPY.mean` with a 5th to 95th percentile range of `{julia} NEMPY.p5` to `{julia} NEMPY.p95`; our percentile range is about three orders of magnitude narrower. We caution against reading this as a ranking: the nempy figures come from a different year, from a sample that under-represents high-demand periods, and nempy takes several inputs (for example the Basslink switch and some constraint right-hand sides) from the NEMDE solution file, which this replica does not.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Published against solved ROP for the 5000 regional prices. Axes use a symmetric pseudo-log scale to show the $-1000$ floor, the bulk near zero and the scarcity tail together; the diagonal is perfect agreement."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5
let
    fig = Figure(size = (880, 700))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Published ROP (\$/MWh)", ylabel = "Solved ROP (\$/MWh)",
        xscale = Makie.pseudolog10, yscale = Makie.pseudolog10, aspect = 1,
        xticks = ([-1000, -100, -10, 0, 10, 100, 1000], string.([-1000, -100, -10, 0, 10, 100, 1000])),
        yticks = ([-1000, -100, -10, 0, 10, 100, 1000], string.([-1000, -100, -10, 0, 10, 100, 1000])))
    lo, hi = -1100, 20000
    lines!(ax, [lo, hi], [lo, hi]; color = :black, linewidth = 1)
    for r in REGIONS
        d = prices[prices.REGIONID .== r, :]
        scatter!(ax, d.ROP_published, d.ROP_solved; color = (REGION_COLOR[r], 0.55), markersize = 6, label = r)
    end
    axislegend(ax; position = :lt, nbanks = 1)
    fig
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-errdist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the signed ROP error. (a) Histogram of the nonzero errors on a log count axis; the central bar holds the exact matches. (b) Empirical CDF of the absolute error; the dotted line marks the 0.001 \\$/MWh agreement threshold and the dashed lines the nempy 5th and 95th percentile magnitudes."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
let
    fig = Figure(size = (1000, 420))
    ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Signed ROP error (\$/MWh)", ylabel = "Regional prices (count)", yscale = log10, title = "(a)")
    edges = range(-3, 3; length = 61)
    h = fit(Histogram, clamp.(e, -3, 3), edges)
    barplot!(ax1, [(edges[i] + edges[i + 1]) / 2 for i in 1:(length(edges) - 1)], max.(h.weights, 0.5); width = step(edges), color = (:steelblue, 0.85), fillto = 0.5)
    ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "Absolute ROP error (\$/MWh)", ylabel = "Share of prices with error ≤ x", xscale = log10, title = "(b)")
    xs = sort(max.(ae, 1.0e-9))
    lines!(ax2, xs, (1:length(xs)) ./ length(xs); linewidth = 2.5, color = :steelblue)
    vlines!(ax2, [EXACT]; color = :gray40, linestyle = :dot)
    vlines!(ax2, [abs(NEMPY.p5), NEMPY.p95]; color = :crimson, linestyle = :dash)
    xlims!(ax2, 1.0e-9, 100)
    ylims!(ax2, 0.9, 1.001)
    fig
end
```

@fig-errdist shows the shape of the residual. The distribution is a spike at zero with thin tails; the CDF reaches `{julia} pct(exact_share)` at the 0.001 \$/MWh agreement threshold and `{julia} pct(mean(ae .< 0.1), d = 2)` at 0.1 \$/MWh.

### Accuracy across the demand range

Because the sample is stratified, accuracy can be read per demand decile without reweighting.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-decile
#| fig-cap: "Price agreement by demand decile (1 = highest-demand tenth of 2025). Left: share of regional prices within 0.001 \\$/MWh. Right: mean absolute error on a log axis. Error is not concentrated at either end of the curve; the largest means come from single intervals (text)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
let
    p = copy(prices)
    p.decile = (p.stratum .- 1) .÷ 100 .+ 1
    g = combine(groupby(p, :decile),
        :error_rop => (v -> mean(abs.(v) .< EXACT)) => :exact,
        :error_rop => (v -> mean(abs.(v))) => :mae,
        :system_demand_mw => mean => :demand)
    sort!(g, :decile)
    fig = Figure(size = (1000, 400))
    ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Demand decile (1 = highest)", ylabel = "Share within 0.001 \$/MWh", xticks = 1:10)
    barplot!(ax1, g.decile, g.exact; color = :steelblue)
    ylims!(ax1, 0.9, 1.0)
    ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "Demand decile (1 = highest)", ylabel = "Mean absolute ROP error (\$/MWh)", yscale = log10, xticks = 1:10)
    barplot!(ax2, g.decile, g.mae; color = :crimson, fillto = 1.0e-5)
    ylims!(ax2, 1.0e-5, 1)
    fig
end
```

# Results: run time

```{julia}
#| output: false
rt.solve_s = rt.execute_s
parts = ["system_build_s", "simulation_build_s", "execute_s", "compare_s"]
labels = ["System build", "Model build", "Solve (both runs)", "Compare"]
means = [mean(rt[!, p]) for p in parts]
total = mean(rt.total_s)
wall_h = 8.5
```

## Where the time goes

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-runtime
#| tbl-cap: "Per-interval run time in seconds (n = 1000 independent solves, six concurrent workers, one HiGHS thread each)."
let
    rows = DataFrame(phase = String[], mean = Float64[], median = Float64[], p95 = Float64[], p99 = Float64[], max = Float64[], share_of_total = Float64[])
    for (p, l) in zip(parts, labels)
        v = rt[!, p]
        push!(rows, (l, mean(v), median(v), q(v, 0.95), q(v, 0.99), maximum(v), mean(v) / total))
    end
    push!(rows, ("Total", total, median(rt.total_s), q(rt.total_s, 0.95), q(rt.total_s, 0.99), maximum(rt.total_s), 1.0))
    mapcols!(c -> c isa Vector{Float64} ? round.(c; sigdigits = 4) : c, rows)
    mdtable(rows)
end
```

A full independent interval costs `{julia} f1(total)` s on average. Constructing the system (`{julia} f1(means[1])` s) and the PSI decision models (`{julia} f1(means[2])` s) accounts for `{julia} pct((means[1] + means[2]) / total, d = 0)` of that; the solve itself, which includes both fast-start runs, result extraction and the dual pass, takes `{julia} f1(means[3])` s on average but only `{julia} f1(median(rt.execute_s))` s at the median. Comparison against the published tables is negligible. The median interval takes `{julia} f1(med_total)` s in total. The mean is inflated by `{julia} n_stall` intervals (`{julia} pct(n_stall / nrow(rt))`) that spend more than five minutes (up to 35) in a single phase (@tbl-runtime): `{julia} stall_by_phase[1]` in system build, `{julia} stall_by_phase[2]` in model build, `{julia} stall_by_phase[3]` in the solve and `{julia} stall_by_phase[4]` in the comparison. Because the stalls are spread over every phase, they look like a machine-level event, not an optimiser effect; we have not established the cause.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-runtime
#| fig-cap: "(a) Mean per-interval time by phase. (b) Histogram of the solve time (log x axis); the long right tail is a few slow intervals. (c) Empirical CDF of total time per interval. All with six workers sharing the machine."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
let
    fig = Figure(size = (1100, 420))
    ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; yticks = (1:4, reverse(labels)), xlabel = "Mean seconds per interval", title = "(a)")
    barplot!(ax1, 1:4, reverse(means); direction = :x, color = reverse(Makie.wong_colors()[1:4]))
    for (i, m) in enumerate(reverse(means))
        text!(ax1, m, i; text = " $(f1(m)) s", align = (:left, :center), fontsize = 12)
    end
    xlims!(ax1, 0, maximum(means) * 1.3)
    ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "Solve time (s)", ylabel = "Intervals", xscale = log10, title = "(b)")
    edges = 10 .^ range(log10(max(minimum(rt.execute_s), 1)), log10(maximum(rt.execute_s)); length = 45)
    h = fit(Histogram, rt.execute_s, edges)
    barplot!(ax2, sqrt.(edges[1:(end - 1)] .* edges[2:end]), h.weights; width = diff(edges), gap = 0, color = (:steelblue, 0.85))
    vlines!(ax2, [median(rt.execute_s), q(rt.execute_s, 0.95)]; color = [:black, :crimson], linestyle = :dash)
    ax3 = Axis(fig[1, 3]; xlabel = "Total time per interval (s)", ylabel = "Share ≤ x", xscale = log10, title = "(c)")
    xs = sort(rt.total_s)
    lines!(ax3, xs, (1:length(xs)) ./ length(xs); linewidth = 2.5, color = :steelblue)
    fig
end
```

The mean MIP time reported by the solver is `{julia} f1(mip_mean)` s and the mean dual solve `{julia} f2(dual_mean)` s, so in a typical interval the optimisation is a small part of the solve phase (`{julia} f1(means[3])` s mean, `{julia} f1(median(rt.execute_s))` s median); the rest is model update, result extraction and writing. The slowest interval, `{julia} s1.interval` with `{julia} fint(s1.execute_s)` s of solve-phase wall time, reports `{julia} f1(s1.timed_solve_time)` s inside the solver, so that time was not spent in HiGHS. This is not true of every slow interval: one of the six slowest, 2025-02-15 06:25, spent 539 s in the MIP itself.

## Throughput and what it means for use

Six workers delivered `{julia} f2(nrow(rt) / (wall_h * 60))` intervals per minute (`{julia} fint(nrow(rt))` intervals in about `{julia} wall_h` hours), a per-interval cost of `{julia} f1(total)` s for each worker slot. Two observations qualify this figure.

First, the cost is dominated by building rather than solving, because each interval here builds a fresh system and model, and in this run reads its time series from an HDF5 file one series at a time (@sec-overheads). This protocol is deliberately the most expensive way to use the code: it pays the full construction cost once per interval so that intervals are statistically independent. In the whole-day mode, a single system and sequence of decision models are built once and stepped through the day with parameter updates, and the same replica solved a 288-interval trading day (2024-12-15) in about 1105 s of wall time in a single process, about 3.8 s per interval, over an uncontended machine. That figure comes from an earlier, separate run, not from the benchmark above, and is not a like-for-like comparison, but it shows the order of magnitude of the amortised cost.

Second, six concurrent processes share one machine and memory bandwidth, so per-process times here are inflated relative to a single uncontended process (our first single-process smoke test took about 50 s per interval). Each worker held about 2.4 to 3.1 GB at peak; six workers used roughly 12 to 15 GB in total with no swapping.

## Runner overheads: process start and time-series storage {#sec-overheads}

The benchmark above ran each trading day in a fresh Julia process and stored the system's time series in an HDF5 file. Two runner changes followed: one persistent worker per shard, and time series held in memory. To measure them, we solved the `{julia} n_ab_int` sampled intervals of `{julia} n_ab_days` trading days spread over 2025 (every 36th trading day of the sample, in date order) twice with the batch runner: once with disk-backed and once with in-memory time series. Each run used one persistent worker on an otherwise idle machine, and the worker's resident set size was sampled every second.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ab_read(mode, name) = CSV.read(joinpath(AB, mode, name), DataFrame; stringtype = String)
ab_rss(mode) = CSV.read(joinpath(AB, "$(mode)_rss.csv"), DataFrame)
ab_first(mode) = minimum(ab_read(mode, "phases.csv").elapsed_s)
function ab_summary(mode)
    days = ab_read(mode, "days.csv")
    first_day, warm = days[1, :], days[2:end, :]
    n = sum(warm.intervals)
    per(c) = sum(warm[!, c]) / n
    return (;
        mode, intervals = sum(days.intervals),
        run_wall_s = TOML.parsefile(joinpath(AB, mode, "outcome.toml"))["elapsed_s"],
        package_load_s = ab_first(mode), first_day_s = first_day.elapsed_s,
        warm_per_interval_s = sum(warm.elapsed_s) / n, system_build_s = per("system_build_s"),
        model_build_s = per("model_build_s"), execute_s = per("execute_s"), highs_s = per("timed_solve_s"),
        peak_rss_mib = maximum(ab_rss(mode).rss_kib) / 1024,
        end_of_day_rss_mib = median(ab_read(mode, "worker_memory.csv").rss_mib),
    )
end
ab = DataFrame([ab_summary(m) for m in ("disk", "memory")])
n_ab_int = ab.intervals[1]
n_ab_days = nrow(ab_read("disk", "days.csv"))
ab_day_prices(mode) = reduce(vcat, [ab_read(mode, joinpath(string(d), "comparison_prices.csv")) for d in ab_read(mode, "days.csv").trading_day])
ab_prices = innerjoin(
    ab_day_prices("disk"), ab_day_prices("memory");
    on = [:SETTLEMENTDATE, :REGIONID], makeunique = true,
)
ab_max_diff = maximum(abs.(ab_prices.ROP_solved .- ab_prices.ROP_solved_1))
ab_speedup = ab.run_wall_s[1] / ab.run_wall_s[2]
ab_warm_speedup = ab.warm_per_interval_s[1] / ab.warm_per_interval_s[2]
ab_rss_delta = ab.peak_rss_mib[2] - ab.peak_rss_mib[1]
# Benchmark cost of one process per day: package load plus the first-interval excess over the day's later intervals.
let r = sort(rt, [:trading_day, :interval])
    r.k = [i == 1 || r.trading_day[i] != r.trading_day[i - 1] ? 1 : 0 for i in 1:nrow(r)]
    global first_excess_s = median(r.total_s[r.k .== 1]) - median(r.total_s[r.k .== 0])
    global n_rt_days = length(unique(r.trading_day))
end
per_day_overhead_h = n_rt_days * (ab.package_load_s[1] + first_excess_s) / 3600
```

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-overheads
#| tbl-cap: "Batch-runner cost of the same sampled intervals with disk-backed and in-memory time series, one persistent worker, one HiGHS thread. Per-interval columns are means over the warm days (every day after the first). Package load is the time to the first phase; the first day includes compilation on first use and is also the heaviest day of the ten."
let
    t = select(
        ab, :mode, :run_wall_s, :package_load_s, :first_day_s, :warm_per_interval_s,
        :system_build_s, :model_build_s, :execute_s, :highs_s, :peak_rss_mib, :end_of_day_rss_mib,
    )
    mapcols!(c -> c isa Vector{Float64} ? round.(c; sigdigits = 4) : c, t)
    mdtable(t)
end
```

Holding the time series in memory makes the run `{julia} f1(ab_speedup)` times faster end to end and a warm interval `{julia} f1(ab_warm_speedup)` times faster (`{julia} f1(ab.warm_per_interval_s[1])` s against `{julia} f1(ab.warm_per_interval_s[2])` s), with identical results: the largest difference between the two runs' `{julia} nrow(ab_prices)` solved regional prices is `{julia} ab_max_diff` \$/MWh. The time saved is in the system build, the model build and the parameter updates inside the solve phase, not in HiGHS (`{julia} f1(ab.highs_s[1])` s and `{julia} f1(ab.highs_s[2])` s per interval). A sampled profile of the disk-backed run located the cost in the time-series storage: InfrastructureSystems opens and closes the HDF5 file for every series it reads when no file handle is held open, and the model build and the parameter updates read one series per component and parameter. Keeping the file open for the whole build and solve (`open_time_series_store!`) was slower still in a separate test, so the in-memory store is the remedy, and it is now the runner's default. Peak resident memory differs by `{julia} f1(ab_rss_delta)` MiB (`{julia} fint(ab.peak_rss_mib[1])` against `{julia} fint(ab.peak_rss_mib[2])` MiB): a sampled interval's time series are small next to the loaded packages and the optimisation models. The end-of-day resident memory, measured after a garbage collection, stays flat across the days of both runs.

The persistent worker saves less. Package loading takes `{julia} f1(ab.package_load_s[2])` s. Compilation on first use shows in the benchmark itself: the first interval of a day took a median `{julia} f1(first_excess_s)` s longer than the day's later intervals, so starting a process for each of the `{julia} n_rt_days` trading days cost about `{julia} f1(per_day_overhead_h)` hours of the `{julia} f1(sum(rt.total_s) / 3600)` process-hours. With both changes, the warm cost of an interval outside the solver falls from `{julia} f1(ab.warm_per_interval_s[1] - ab.highs_s[1])` s to `{julia} f1(ab.warm_per_interval_s[2] - ab.highs_s[2])` s on an idle machine. The run-time figures of @tbl-runtime, measured with the old runner and six workers sharing the machine, therefore overstate the cost of the current runner.

# Sources of difference from NEMDE {#sec-sources}

`{julia} nint_diff` of the `{julia} fint(n_int)` intervals (`{julia} pct(nint_diff / n_int)`) have at least one regional price that differs from the published ROP by more than 0.001 \$/MWh. To understand them we classify each by whether the dispatch also differs. If every unit's dispatch target and every interconnector flow matches NEMDE but the price does not, the primal solution is the same and the difference must come from the dual. Such a difference may be a tie in the offer stack, which @sec-dualrange tests. If the dispatch also differs, the primal solutions differ.

```{julia}
#| output: false
function interval_diag(prices, disp2, ic2)
    pmax = combine(groupby(prices, :SETTLEMENTDATE), :error_rop => (v -> maximum(abs.(v))) => :max_price_err,
        :system_demand_mw => first => :demand)
    dmax = combine(groupby(disp2, :SETTLEMENTDATE), :diff => (v -> maximum(abs.(v))) => :max_dispatch_diff_mw)
    fmax = combine(groupby(ic2, :SETTLEMENTDATE), :fdiff => (v -> maximum(abs.(v))) => :max_flow_diff_mw)
    d = leftjoin(leftjoin(pmax, dmax; on = :SETTLEMENTDATE), fmax; on = :SETTLEMENTDATE)
    return d
end
diag = interval_diag(prices, disp2, ic2)
diag.class = map(eachrow(diag)) do r
    r.max_price_err <= EXACT && return "match"
    pd = coalesce(r.max_dispatch_diff_mw, 0.0)
    fd = coalesce(r.max_flow_diff_mw, 0.0)
    return (pd <= 0.5 && fd <= 0.5) ? "same dispatch, different price" : "different dispatch"
end
cls = combine(groupby(diag, :class), nrow => :intervals, :max_price_err => (v -> maximum(v)) => :largest_price_error)
n_same = count(==("same dispatch, different price"), diag.class)
n_diffd = count(==("different dispatch"), diag.class)
```

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-classes
#| tbl-cap: "Classification of the 1000 intervals. 'Same dispatch' means every matched unit is within 0.5 MW and every interconnector flow within 0.5 MW of NEMDE."
mdtable(cls)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-diag
#| fig-cap: "Largest price error against the largest dispatch difference in each interval that disagrees on price (log-log). Points at the left edge match NEMDE's dispatch almost exactly and differ only in the dual; the large-error points that sit to the right have different dispatch."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
let
    d = filter(r -> r.max_price_err > EXACT, diag)
    fig = Figure(size = (880, 540))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Largest unit dispatch difference in the interval (MW, +0.001)", ylabel = "Largest |price error| in the interval (\$/MWh)", xscale = log10, yscale = log10)
    scatter!(ax, coalesce.(d.max_dispatch_diff_mw, 0.0) .+ 1.0e-3, d.max_price_err; color = (:crimson, 0.7), markersize = 9)
    vlines!(ax, [0.5]; color = :gray40, linestyle = :dash)
    fig
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-worst
#| tbl-cap: "The fifteen intervals with the largest price error, with the largest dispatch and flow differences in the same interval."
let
    d = sort(filter(r -> r.max_price_err > EXACT, diag), :max_price_err; rev = true)
    mdtable(first(select(d, :SETTLEMENTDATE, :max_price_err, :max_dispatch_diff_mw, :max_flow_diff_mw, :demand, :class), 15))
end
```

## Family 1: ties in the offer stack

`{julia} n_same` intervals have the same dispatch as NEMDE but a different price. Most differ by well under 0.1 \$/MWh. Two do not: 2025-06-16 10:45 in South Australia (1.17 \$/MWh, where one unit's dispatch differs by 0.14 MW) and 2025-07-07 12:15 in Tasmania, where AEMSim's price is `{julia} f2(showcase.solved_benchmark)` \$/MWh and NEMDE's is `{julia} f2(showcase.published)` \$/MWh, a difference of `{julia} f2(showcase.solved_benchmark - showcase.published)` \$/MWh. We examine the larger one.

Dispatch is identical for all 518 unit rows and the interconnector flows agree, so the difference is entirely in the dual. AEMO's published NEMDE case files for the interval (the loaded case and the price-setter file, both available on NEMWEB) show why. NEMDE's price setter output decomposes each regional price into the unit bands that would move if one more MW of demand were served:

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-pricesetter
#| tbl-cap: "NEMDE price-setter entries for the TAS1 energy price in the interval ending 2025-07-07 12:15, from AEMO's published price-setter file. 'Increase' is the change in the unit's dispatch for one more MW of regional demand, 'RRNBandPrice' the band price referred to the regional reference node, and 'BandCost' their product. The costs sum to the published price."
let
    path = joinpath(RUN, "nemde_xml", "NEMPriceSetter_2025070709900.xml")
    if isfile(path)
        txt = read(path, String)
        rows = DataFrame(unit = String[], market = String[], band = String[], increase = Float64[], band_price = Float64[], band_cost = Float64[])
        for m in eachmatch(r"RegionID=\"TAS1\" Market=\"Energy\" Price=\"([\d.]+)\" Unit=\"([^\"]+)\" DispatchedMarket=\"([^\"]+)\" BandNo=\"(\d+)\" Increase=\"([-\d.]+)\" RRNBandPrice=\"([-\d.]+)\" BandCost=\"([-\d.]+)\"", txt)
            push!(rows, (m[2], m[3], m[4], parse(Float64, m[5]), parse(Float64, m[6]), parse(Float64, m[7])))
        end
        push!(rows, ("Sum", "", "", NaN, NaN, sum(rows.band_cost)))
        mdtable(rows)
    else
        Markdown.parse("NEMDE price-setter file not found under `$(RUN)/nemde_xml`.")
    end
end
```

The Basslink interconnector (`T-V-MNSP1`) is a price setter on the TAS1-side offer band at 57.42 \$/MWh. Its TAS1 offer holds 55 MW at band 4 and 50 MW at band 5, so the cumulative offer through band 5 ends exactly at 105 MW (band 6 offers a further 333 MW at a higher price). NEMDE's solution has the flow at $-104.99987$ MW, just inside band 5 by 0.00013 MW, so band 5 is the marginal band and sets the price. AEMSim's flow is $-105.0$ MW: exactly the band edge. At the edge, the lower band and the next source (a Tasmanian generator whose band begins at 190.04 \$/MWh) both set a price that the offer stack can produce. The price-setter file points to a tie at the band edge, and HiGHS may have returned a different vertex from NEMDE's.

The same interval shows the same pattern in a second market. TAS1 `RAISEREG` is 7.24 \$/MW in AEMSim against 6.24 \$/MW published. NEMDE's price-setter file names `TUNGATIN` at band 3 (6.24), and that unit clears 22 MW against a 22 MW band: again exactly the band edge, and again NEMDE reports the lower band. AEMO's constraint FAQ specifies pro-rata tie-breaking for price-tied *energy* bands and states that it does not apply to FCAS [@aemo_constraint_faq], so the FCAS case at least has no specified rule.

Two cautions apply. First, this is one interval, and other intervals with differing prices have solved prices *lower* than published (for example 2025-06-16 SA1, 2025-07-26 TAS1, 2025-11-01 QLD1), so no single direction of bias explains them. Second, we do not know why NEMDE lands 0.00013 MW inside the band; it may be solver tolerance rather than a rule. Whether this price is degenerate depends on the finer step. Across the 0.0001 MW step the price runs from `{julia} f2(sc_lo)` to `{julia} f2(sc_hi)` \$/MWh. The probe classifies the published `{julia} f2(showcase.published)` \$/MWh as `{julia} showcase.distance` (@sec-dualrange). `{julia} sc_in ? "The published price lies within the model's optimal-price range at 0.0001 MW of the operating point, so this difference is degeneracy and not evidence of model error." : "The published price is not reached within 0.0001 MW, so this difference is not degeneracy at that size."}`

The vertex chosen at a tie in the offer stack does not depend on the inputs alone. A refactor of system construction, checked outside this benchmark on ten sampled intervals, moved FCAS prices at two of them, and a later change moved them back. At both intervals the runs before and after the refactor have the same objective, the same dispatch for every unit, and the same interconnector flows and energy prices. At 2025-04-29 22:15, the system built before the refactor and the one built after the later change hold identical values in all 18,678 of their time series. Mainland `RAISEREG` at 2025-04-29 22:15 went from 18.65 to 17.53 \$/MW (published 17.53) and back to 18.65. TAS1 `LOWERREG` at 2025-03-11 16:00 went from 3.31 to 2.82 (published 2.49) and back to 3.31. With the solver and its options unchanged, the order in which the model is assembled is enough to change which optimal dual HiGHS returns. An FCAS price that moves closer to or further from NEMDE while the primal solution is unchanged therefore says nothing about model fidelity, and we compare code revisions on inputs, objective and dispatch first.

## Family 2: genuinely different dispatch

`{julia} n_diffd` intervals have a dispatch difference above 0.5 MW in some unit or a flow difference above 0.5 MW. These include the largest price errors, and we have not diagnosed them to the same depth as the tie in family 1. The facts are:

- **2025-06-18 18:20.** The largest error in the sample: VIC1, NSW1, SA1 and QLD1 ROPs are 33 to 57 \$/MWh above published, at published prices of about 590 to 1000 \$/MWh and a system demand of 32.0 GW (the second-highest in the sample). The largest unit difference is 9.5 MW (`CAPBES1`, a battery) and the largest interconnector flow difference 2.3 MW. This is a scarcity interval, where small changes in which constraints violate or which FCAS requirements are met move prices.
- **2025-03-06 18:40.** `BRAEMAR6` differs by 154 MW although all interconnector flows match to 0.004 MW and the price error is 0.1 \$/MWh: an offer or limit that NEMDE treats differently, or an alternative optimum among equal-cost options.
- **2025-02-21 23:35, 2025-06-26 21:00, 2025-06-14 18:20, 2025-12-31 20:30, 2025-11-12 17:50.** Unit differences of 13 to 28 MW and flow differences of 1 to 31 MW, with price errors between 0.6 and 3 \$/MWh.

Without NEMDE's objective value in the published tables we cannot say whether these dispatches are equal-cost alternatives (a primal degeneracy) or whether the replica's feasible set differs from NEMDE's through an input, a constraint term or a tolerance. We list them as targets for case-by-case analysis against the loaded NEMDE case file, which carries the full input set and solution.

## Family 2b: a violated FCAS requirement that the energy-price classification misses

The classification above is by energy price, so it cannot see an FCAS-only difference. One interval stands out when the FCAS prices are compared: 2025-03-17 01:20. AEMSim violates both Tasmanian regulation requirement constraints (`F_T+LREG_0050` and `F_T+RREG_0050`, each by the full 50 MW) and therefore prices TAS1 `RAISEREG` and `LOWERREG` at the violated-requirement level, 175,008 and 175,002 \$/MW, against 8.27 and 2.26 published. Energy prices match NEMDE in all five regions (TAS1 is 355.02 in both) and the interval is not among the `{julia} nint_diff` price-differing intervals. The replica finds Tasmanian regulation capacity short where NEMDE does not; we have not found why. It is the only FCAS price error above 12 \$/MW in the sample, and it alone produces the regulation-service means in @tbl-fcas.

## Family 3: gaps in the source data {#sec-data}

AEMO's September 2025 `DISPATCHLOAD` and `DISPATCH_MNSPBIDTRK` archive files end at 2025-09-30 04:00. NEMWEB lists only a first file for that month, and its last record, followed by a normal end-of-report footer, is the 04:00 interval; the remainder of the month's last day is absent from the source. This is not a download fault. Eleven of the first draw (1.1%) fell on the affected trading days and could not be built; the benchmark's resampling step replaces failed intervals from the same stratum on other days. We mention it because any validation against the MMSDM archive inherits its gaps, and because the pipeline fails loudly on the missing rows instead of filling them.

## Testing the degeneracy explanation {#sec-dualrange}

Where the LP has several optimal duals, the price it reports depends on the vertex the solver returns, and no formulation can be expected to reproduce NEMDE's choice. For energy, AEMO's tie-break constraint (item 53 of the schedule of constraint violation penalty factors) resolves dispatch among price-tied offers [@aemo_cvp_schedule], and NEMDE's tie-break rows apply to energy offers only [@aemo_constraint_faq]. AEMO publishes no selection rule for FCAS prices, so an FCAS tie has no rule for a formulation to reproduce. Differences of this kind are therefore not evidence of model error. The question is how many of the remaining differences are of this kind.

A price difference is explained by degeneracy only if AEMO's published price is itself an optimal price of our model. This can be tested directly. For an LP with its binaries fixed, the optimal cost is a convex, piecewise-linear function of the right-hand side of any row, and the set of optimal duals of that row is the interval between its left and right slopes. We re-solved every interval with a differing energy or FCAS price, fixed the binaries at the optimum as the dual pass does, and moved the right-hand side of the rows behind each differing price by ±h MW for each h in `{julia} join(H_MW, ", ")`: the regional energy balance for an energy price, or every FCAS requirement constraint of that region and service for an FCAS price, whose summed dual is the regional FCAS price as in `DISPATCH_FCAS_REQ`. The dual of each moved LP is the price on that side. A price is labelled degenerate (h MW) when it lies between the two sides at h. That means it is an optimal price of our model within ±h MW of its operating point, not at it. If it is reached only at a larger h, our model would produce it with that much more or less demand or requirement, so the published price sits at a nearby breakpoint and the difference is not explained by degeneracy at that size. The probe is `scripts/dual_range_probe.jl`, and its output `dual_ranges.csv` is read here.

Of the `{julia} fint(nrow(dr_all))` probed prices, `{julia} n_failed` failed or returned no rows and are excluded, and `{julia} n_fixed_bad` more are excluded because the re-solved price lies outside the optimal-dual range of their fixed LP (`fixed_lp_matches == false`), so the re-solve fixed different binaries. The remaining `{julia} fint(n_probe)` energy and FCAS prices differ from the published value by more than 0.001 in their unit (\$/MWh for energy, \$/MW for FCAS) in `{julia} fint(n_probe_int)` intervals. The probe classifies them in @tbl-dualrange.

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-dualrange
#| tbl-cap: "Differing prices by the smallest right-hand-side move, in MW, at which the published price becomes an optimal price of the model. 'Degenerate (h MW)' rows are optimal prices of the model within h MW of its operating point; the other rows need the demand or requirement to move by up to the stated amount. Absolute errors are |solved minus published|, in \\$/MWh for energy and \\$/MW for FCAS."
let
    g = combine(groupby(dr, [:distance, :kind]), nrow => :n)
    w = unstack(g, :kind, :n; fill = 0)
    for k in ("energy", "FCAS")
        k in names(w) || (w[!, k] = zeros(Int, nrow(w)))
    end
    m = combine(groupby(dr, :distance), nrow => :all, :abs_error => (v -> round(median(v); sigdigits = 3)) => :median_abs_error,
        :abs_error => (v -> round(maximum(v); sigdigits = 3)) => :max_abs_error)
    t = leftjoin(m, w; on = :distance)
    t.order = indexin(t.distance, DR_ORDER)
    sort!(t, :order)
    mdtable(select(t, :distance, :energy, :FCAS, :all, :median_abs_error, :max_abs_error))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: tbl-dualrange-market
#| tbl-cap: "Differing prices by market and class."
let
    g = combine(groupby(dr, [:market, :distance]), nrow => :n)
    w = unstack(g, :distance, :n; fill = 0)
    cols = [c for c in DR_ORDER if c in names(w)]
    mdtable(sort(select(w, :market, cols...), :market))
end
```

Degeneracy does not account for all the differences. `{julia} n_degen` of the `{julia} n_probe` prices (`{julia} pct(n_degen / n_probe)`) are degenerate at 0.0001 MW, and in `{julia} n_iv_degen` of the `{julia} n_probe_int` intervals every differing price is. These are the regulation and contingency patterns that look like ties:

- **Tasmanian regulation.** `{julia} n_tasreg_degen` of the `{julia} nrow(tasreg)` TAS1 `RAISEREG` and `LOWERREG` prices that differ by about 1 \$/MW are degenerate. Those that are degenerate are the band-edge ties of @tbl-pricesetter, where the model admits every price between two adjacent FCAS bands and NEMDE reported the other band.
- **Lower contingency pairs.** `{julia} n_lswap_degen` of the `{julia} nrow(lswap)` `LOWER6SEC` and `LOWER60SEC` prices are degenerate. In `{julia} n_lpairs_opp` of the `{julia} n_lpairs` (interval, region) pairs with both services, the two errors sum to within 0.001 \$/MW of zero. An offer that serves both services makes only the sum of the two prices unique, which would produce that pattern.

Re-solving the same interval moves the price. `{julia} nrow(moved)` of the differing prices change when the interval is solved again, and `{julia} moved_to_pub` of them then match the published price exactly. Every benchmark price but `{julia} n_probe - bench_in_range` is an optimal price of the re-solved model at 0.0001 MW, so for those the benchmark and the re-solve picked different optimal prices of the same problem. The exceptions are in `{julia} bench_out_ints`.

The `{julia} n_small` prices (`{julia} pct(n_small / n_probe)`) are reached only more than 0.0001 MW and at most 0.01 MW from the operating point. The other `{julia} n_far` (`{julia} pct(n_far / n_probe)`) are further away, and for these NEMDE's price is not an optimal price of our model within 0.01 MW of its operating point, so degeneracy at that size does not explain them. The mainland raise contingency services carry `{julia} nrow(mainland_raise)` of the prices outside TAS1, `{julia} pct(count(!=(DR_ORDER[1]), mainland_raise.distance) / nrow(mainland_raise))` of them not degenerate. For `{julia} flat10` of the `{julia} n_rest` non-degenerate prices our price does not move under a 10 MW change in the demand or requirement. NEMDE's price is then not reached within 10 MW, so NEMDE and the replica clear a different marginal band or unit. That points to a difference in offers, availability or requirement inputs, not to the choice of dual. For energy, `{julia} n_ergy_10` of the `{julia} n_ergy_rest` non-degenerate energy prices become NEMDE's price within 1 to 10 MW of demand, which is consistent with small differences in offered or available MW. We have not diagnosed these differences.

Two limits apply to the test. It probes one price at a time, so a degenerate price is shown to be an optimal price on its own, not that NEMDE's whole price vector is optimal for our model; for the non-degenerate prices this does not matter, since failing on one price is enough. It also holds the binaries at the re-solved optimum. NEMDE may fix interconnector loss segments or MNSP directions differently at the same objective, which would give a different LP. The benchmark price is not an optimal price of the re-solved model at 0.0001 MW for the `{julia} n_probe - bench_in_range` prices in `{julia} bench_out_ints`, so there the two solves produced different fixed LPs, through different binaries or through code changes since the benchmark commit. Such a change of LP cannot account for the `{julia} n_beyond10` prices that remain beyond 10 MW.

Degenerate differences need no model change, since no formulation can be expected to choose NEMDE's vertex among equal optima. The non-degenerate ones need further investigation, and the per-price classification in `dual_ranges.csv` says which is which.

## Differences that are not model error

Four methodological points affect any comparison of this kind.

- **Price definition.** We compare the solved price with the published ROP, the regional reference price before post-dispatch adjustment, as nempy does, and not the settled RRP, which includes scaling and capping.
- **Tolerance.** The agreement threshold of 0.001 \$/MWh is far above solver precision. HiGHS is run at a relative MIP gap of $10^{-9}$; we do not know the tolerances NEMDE's solver uses. Differences of the order of $10^{-4}$ \$/MWh to $10^{-2}$ \$/MWh should not be read as model error.
- **Dual-only differences.** Where the optimum is degenerate (@sec-dualrange), the reported price is one of several valid duals, and which one is returned can change with solver options or with the order the model is built in (@sec-sources, family 1). FCAS prices are the most exposed, since AEMO publishes no selection rule for them.
- **Unmatched rows.** A small share of unit rows exist in only one side of the comparison (for example units without a published `TOTALCLEARED`); they are excluded and counted.

## Comparison with nempy's benchmark

nempy's benchmark reports a mean signed error of `{julia} NEMPY.mean` \$/MWh with a median of 0 and 5th to 95th percentiles of `{julia} NEMPY.p5` and `{julia} NEMPY.p95` on 1000 uniform intervals of 2024 H2. Our numbers are lower in the mean, with a far tighter percentile range. The two are not like-for-like for four reasons: (i) a different year and a different regulatory context (five-minute settlement, new FCAS markets, different constraint equations); (ii) uniform against demand-stratified sampling; (iii) nempy takes some inputs from the NEMDE case file where this replica rebuilds them from MMSDM; (iv) differences in formulation and solver, which affect how dual degeneracy is resolved. The most defensible conclusion is the weaker one: a replica built purely from the public MMSDM tables reproduces NEMDE's prices to within 0.001 \$/MWh in about 99% of regional prices and diverges materially in a small number of well-characterised situations.

# Relation to the design of PowerSimulations.jl

The benchmark exercises the whole stack, and the way the replica is expressed in PSI is part of why it is tractable.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[NEMWEB MMSDM archives] --> B[Data package: populate]
    B --> C[(Hive parquet cache, DuckDB)]
    C --> D["AEM: nem_system(NEMDEConfiguration)"]
    D --> E[PSY System: stock devices + NEMUnitData attributes + time series]
    E --> F["AEMSim: template_nemde / DecisionModel(NEMDispatchProblem)"]
    F --> G[PSI + JuMP + HiGHS]
    G --> H[Results readers]
    H --> I[Comparison with published NEMDE outcomes]
    C --> I
```

**Separation of inputs and model.** The root package writes every NEMDE input once, in `nem_system`, as typed attributes and time series on stock PowerSystems.jl devices; the simulation package only reads them. A device is a NEMDE unit when it carries a `NEMUnitData` supplemental attribute, not because of its type, so the same `System` can hold conventional units, batteries, wind and solar, hydro and scheduled loads. PSI's separation between the `System` (data), the `ProblemTemplate` (which formulation applies to which device type and which services and network model are used) and the `DecisionModel` (the optimisation problem) is what lets NEMDE's formulation be expressed as device, service and constraint formulations without special-casing the data layer.

**NEM-specific formulations as PSI extensions.** NEMDE is not a standard unit-commitment: offers are price bands with an additional availability and ramp envelope, FCAS enablement follows trapezia coupled to energy through joint capacity and ramp constraints, losses are modelled piecewise and referred to the regional reference node, tie-breaking constraints share price-tied bands, thousands of generic constraints carry constraint violation penalty factors, and fast-start units follow an inflexibility profile in a two-run solve. Each of these is an `AbstractNEMDispatch` device formulation, a service or a constraint formulation registered through the template, and the keyword builder `template_nemde` assembles them. Because they are ordinary PSI constructs, results come back through PSI's results interface and the same machinery supports closed-loop simulation, in which each interval starts from the previous solution instead of AEMO's observed state.

**Fit with PSI's execution model.** The independent-interval protocol used here is a one-step simulation per interval; the whole-day and closed-loop modes use a multi-step `Simulation`. The measured construction-versus-solve split shows the cost of PSI's strength and of the protocol: building a model is expensive relative to solving a five-minute dispatch, so the amortised multi-step mode, in which parameters update in place, is the right way to produce many consecutive intervals. The benchmark's per-interval build is the price of statistical independence, not the cost of the intended use.

**Dependencies and portability.** The simulation package currently depends on a pinned fork of PowerSimulations (and the root package on forks of InfrastructureSystems and HDF5). The simulation package cannot be registered until the fork's changes are released upstream, which bounds how far the replica is portable today.

# Reproducibility {.unnumbered}

```{julia}
#| echo: false
let
    o = manifest["options"]
    println("Run folder:    ", RUN)
    println("Created:       ", manifest["created"])
    println("Julia:         ", manifest["julia"])
    println("Git commit:    ", manifest["git_commit"], " (the benchmark scripts were uncommitted)")
    println("Probe commit:  ", join(unique(dr_all.git_commit), ", "))
    println("Year / seed:   ", o["year"], " / ", o["seed"])
    println("Workers:       ", o["workers"], " (HiGHS threads each: ", o["solver-threads"], ")")
end
```

The benchmark runs in six steps. Steps 1 and 2 populate the cache, draw the load-duration-stratified sample, solve it in parallel shards and write the analysis files that this notebook reads. Step 3 builds the probe targets from those files, step 4 probes the optimal-price ranges of the differing prices, step 5 measures the runner overheads and step 6 renders this report. Set `AEM_RUNTIME_AB_RUN` to read the overhead measurement from another folder.

```sh
# 1. populate the cache, draw the sample and solve it in parallel shards
julia -O1 --project=AustralianElectricityMarketsSimulations/test scripts/nempy_benchmark.jl \
    --populate true --workers 6 --output "$HOME/aem_validation/ldc-2025"
# 2. redraw and solve the failed intervals (source gaps)
julia -O1 --project=AustralianElectricityMarketsSimulations/test scripts/nempy_benchmark.jl \
    --resample true --workers 6 --output "$HOME/aem_validation/ldc-2025"
```

```julia
# 3. build the probe targets (interval, market, region, published, solved) from the analysis files
using CSV, DataFrames
analysis = joinpath(homedir(), "aem_validation", "ldc-2025", "analysis")
prices = CSV.read(joinpath(analysis, "price_errors.csv"), DataFrame)
fcas = CSV.read(joinpath(analysis, "fcas_errors.csv"), DataFrame)
energy = filter(r -> !ismissing(r.error_rop) && abs(r.error_rop) > 0.001, prices)
fcas_diff = filter(r -> !ismissing(r.ROP_solved) && !ismissing(r.ROP_published) && abs(r.ROP_solved - r.ROP_published) > 0.001, fcas)
targets = vcat(
    DataFrame(interval = energy.SETTLEMENTDATE, market = "ENERGY", region = energy.REGIONID,
        published = energy.ROP_published, solved = energy.ROP_solved),
    DataFrame(interval = fcas_diff.SETTLEMENTDATE, market = fcas_diff.BIDTYPE, region = fcas_diff.REGIONID,
        published = fcas_diff.ROP_published, solved = fcas_diff.ROP_solved),
)
CSV.write(joinpath(analysis, "targets.csv"), targets)
```

```sh
# 4. probe the optimal-price range of each differing price
julia -O1 --project=AustralianElectricityMarketsSimulations/test scripts/dual_range_probe.jl \
    "$HOME/aem_validation/ldc-2025/analysis/targets.csv" \
    "$HOME/aem_validation/ldc-2025/analysis/dual_ranges.csv"
```

If the targets are split into parts and probed separately, each writing its own output file in `analysis/dual_parts/`, stack the parts with their headers read rather than concatenating text:

```julia
using CSV, DataFrames
analysis = joinpath(homedir(), "aem_validation", "ldc-2025", "analysis")
files = filter(endswith(".csv"), readdir(joinpath(analysis, "dual_parts"); join = true))
CSV.write(joinpath(analysis, "dual_ranges.csv"), reduce(vcat, [CSV.read(f, DataFrame) for f in files]))
```

```sh
# 5. the runner-overhead measurement (@sec-overheads): ten spread trading days, disk then memory
julia --project=docs -e 'using DuckDB, DataFrames, Dates
    s = DataFrame(DuckDB.execute(DuckDB.DB(), "SELECT interval FROM read_csv(\'$(homedir())/aem_validation/ldc-2025/analysis/ldc_sample.csv\') ORDER BY interval"))
    s.day = Date.(s.interval .- Minute(5) .- Hour(4)); days = sort(unique(s.day))[1:36:end]
    mkpath(joinpath(homedir(), "aem_validation", "runtime-ab"))
    open(joinpath(homedir(), "aem_validation", "runtime-ab", "intervals.csv"), "w") do io
        println(io, "interval"); foreach(t -> println(io, Dates.format(t, "yyyy-mm-ddTHH:MM:SS")), s.interval[in.(s.day, Ref(days))])
    end'
for mode in disk memory; do
    julia -O1 --project=AustralianElectricityMarketsSimulations/test scripts/batch_run.jl \
        --intervals-file "$HOME/aem_validation/runtime-ab/intervals.csv" --hours 24 \
        --time-series-in-memory $([ $mode = memory ] && echo true || echo false) \
        --output "$HOME/aem_validation/runtime-ab/$mode" &
    # sample the worker's resident set size every second while the run lasts
    echo "t_s,pid,rss_kib" > "$HOME/aem_validation/runtime-ab/${mode}_rss.csv"; t0=$(date +%s)
    while kill -0 $! 2>/dev/null; do
        for pid in $(pgrep -f "worker-loop $HOME/aem_validation/runtime-ab/$mode"); do
            echo "$(( $(date +%s) - t0 )),$pid,$(ps -o rss= -p $pid | tr -d ' ')" >> "$HOME/aem_validation/runtime-ab/${mode}_rss.csv"
        done; sleep 1
    done
done
```

```sh
# 6. this report
quarto render benchmarking/report/ldc_benchmark.qmd
```

Set `AEM_BENCHMARK_RUN` to render the notebook against another run folder.
